fields.h1: What Does the Bible Say About the End Times?
fields.meta_title: What Does the Bible Say About the End Times?
fields.description: Beneath the speculation, the Bible is clear: Christ will return, the dead will be raised, and God will make all things new. What Scripture actually says about the end.
fields.body_html:
Few subjects stir as much curiosity — and as much confusion — as the end times. Books, films, and headlines feed endless speculation about dates, signs, and cataclysms. Christians themselves hold different views on some of the details, and the debates can be fierce. It is easy to get so lost in the disputed questions that we miss the clear and comforting hope at the centre. But beneath the disputed questions lies a solid core on which the Bible is wonderfully clear, and that core is not a timetable of disasters but a Person: Jesus Christ will return. The Christian hope for the future is not fear but a Saviour — “our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13). Here is what Scripture actually says, sifted from the speculation.

Jesus will return — personally and visibly

The central truth of the end times is the return of Christ. Just as he came the first time in humility, he will come again in glory. As the disciples watched him ascend, angels promised, “This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11). His return will not be a private or symbolic event but a personal, visible, unmistakable coming — “the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command” (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

This is the anchor of Christian hope for the future. History is not a meaningless cycle or a slow fade into nothing; it is moving toward a climax — the day when the King returns to put everything right. Whatever the darkness of the present age, the believer looks forward not to catastrophe but to Christ. He promised his troubled disciples, “I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also” (John 14:3). The end of the story is not the end of the world but the arrival of its rightful King.

No one knows the day or the hour

Here Scripture is blunt, and it cuts through a vast amount of speculation: no one knows when. Jesus said plainly, “concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only” (Matthew 24:36). Every attempt to calculate a date for his return runs directly against his words, and every such prediction has failed, as it must.

Because the time is hidden, Jesus’ repeated command is not to calculate but to be ready: “Therefore, stay awake, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming... Therefore you also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect” (Matthew 24:42, 44). The point of prophecy is not to satisfy our curiosity but to shape our lives — to keep us watchful, faithful, and living each day as those who will give account. A Christian preoccupied with charts and dates has missed the purpose; a Christian living ready has grasped it.

The dead will be raised and believers transformed

When Christ returns, one of the great events Scripture promises is the resurrection of the dead. Death is not the end for those in Christ; their bodies will be raised and glorified. “The Lord himself will descend from heaven... And the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive... will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). In an instant everything will change: “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet... the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:52).

This is why Christians can face death, including the death of those they love, with grief but not despair. The grave is a temporary bed, not a final home. The same Jesus who rose bodily from the tomb will raise his people, giving them glorified, deathless bodies fit for the new creation. Every believer who has ever died will stand again, whole and radiant, on that day. That hope robs death of its final power.

There will be a final judgment

Scripture also teaches that Christ’s return brings judgment — the setting right of all wrongs. “When the Son of Man comes in his glory... he will separate people one from another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats” (Matthew 25:31–32). Every life will be brought into the light, every injustice addressed, every secret exposed. This is sobering, but it is also deeply hopeful: it means evil does not have the last word, and the God of justice will finally judge the world in righteousness.

For those who are in Christ, the judgment holds no condemnation, for their sins were already judged at the cross; they will be welcomed home. For those who have refused God’s mercy, it is a solemn reckoning. This is why the message of the end times is finally a call to be ready now — to turn to Christ while there is time, since God “is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). The delay of Christ’s return is not slackness but mercy, giving room for people to come to him.

Reading the signs rightly

Jesus did speak of signs that would mark the age before his return — but he framed them to steady his followers, not to alarm them. “And you will hear of wars and rumors of wars. See that you are not alarmed, for this must take place, but the end is not yet” (Matthew 24:6). He spoke of conflict, famine, deception, persecution, and false messiahs, and then added the one sign tied to his purpose: “this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come” (Matthew 24:14).

Two errors are worth avoiding here. One is to read every headline as a coded countdown, anxiously matching current events to prophecy — a preoccupation Jesus never encouraged. The other is to grow complacent, living as though he will never come. The signs are given not so we can predict the date, but so we are not caught off guard and not shaken when hard things come. Wars, disasters, and opposition are not evidence that God has lost control; Jesus said they “must take place.” The believer reads the times with a steady heart, keeps proclaiming the gospel, and watches for the King.

The end is a new beginning — a renewed creation

The Bible’s vision of the end is not annihilation but renewal. The story climaxes not in a smoking ruin but in a new creation, where God dwells with his people forever. John saw “a new heaven and a new earth,” and heard the promise: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away” (Revelation 21:1, 4). This is the true end of the end times — everything sad come untrue, and everything good made permanent.

So the Christian looks forward not with dread but with longing. The present world, with all its beauty and all its brokenness, will give way to a world made new, purified of every evil and filled with the presence of God. The details of how we get there Christians may debate, but the destination is not in doubt: a restored creation, an unbroken fellowship with God, and joy without end.

How then should we live?

The Bible’s teaching on the end times is intensely practical. It is given not to frighten or to fuel speculation, but to change how we live now. Peter draws the conclusion directly: since these things are coming, “what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness” (2 Peter 3:11). The certainty of Christ’s return should make us watchful, holy, and busy about his work — living ready, loving well, and telling others while there is time.

So do not be consumed by charts, dates, or fear. Fix your hope on the returning King, keep your life ready to meet him, and let the certainty of that day steady you through every trouble of this one. “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20) is the fitting prayer of every believer — not a cry of terror, but of longing for the Saviour who is coming to make all things new. The end of the story is very good news for all who belong to him. Make sure, then, that you belong to him — for the surest preparation for the end times is not a stockpile of predictions but a heart that is ready, resting in Christ and longing for his appearing.
